It sounds like you're feeling really stressed about this maths test, especially since fractions haven't quite clicked yet. Instead of skipping it, here are a few practical ways you can handle this right now:

Talk to your teacher: Go to them before class (or send a quick email) and say, "I've been studying fractions, and I'm still struggling to understand how equivalent fractions work. Is there any chance I could get a bit of extra help or retake this once I get the hang of it?" Teachers almost always appreciate honesty and are much more willing to help when you ask upfront.

Tell your mum: Let her know you're feeling overwhelmed by the test. She might be able to help you study tonight or reach out to your teacher directly to explain that you're struggling with the material.

Keep practicing with me: We can take a break from the rules and try a completely different approach—like drawing it out with blocks or doing a quick 5-minute practice run—so you feel more confident walking into class.

transcript.text:
The missing number is 4, so 2/3 = 4/6.

How to solve it:
Look at the denominators (the bottom numbers): to get from 3 to 6, you multiply by 2 (3 × 2 = 6).
Do the same to the numerator (the top number) to keep the fractions equal: 2 × 2 = 4.
I get that the answer is four, but I do not understand why you have to multiply the top number as well.

Think of a pizza cut into 3 large slices, and you eat 2 of them (2/3 of the pizza).

Now, imagine you take each of those 3 slices and cut them right down the middle into 2 smaller pieces.

Bottom number (total slices): Since every single slice was cut in half, the whole pizza now has 6 slices (3 × 2 = 6).
Top number (your slices): Because the 2 slices you ate were also cut in half, you now have 4 smaller pieces (2 × 2 = 4).

You are still eating the exact same amount of pizza—you just chopped it into twice as many pieces. Because the pieces are half the size, you need twice as many of them to equal the same amount.

The "Multiplying by 1" Rule
In math, multiplying any number by 1 never changes its value (for example, 5 × 1 = 5).

A fraction where the top and bottom numbers are the same—like 2/2—is equal to 1 whole. So when you multiply both the top and bottom by 2, you are really just multiplying your fraction by 1 in disguise:
2/3 × 1 = 2/3 × 2/2 = 4/6

If you only multiplied the bottom number, you would be changing the actual amount (2/6 is much less pizza than 2/3!).
I get that the answer is four, but I still do not understand why you have to multiply both numbers by the same amount.

Think of a fraction as a comparison—specifically, a ratio of "what you have" to "what makes a whole."

If you only change the bottom number, you are changing the size of the whole without updating your share to match.

Look at what happens if you DON'T multiply both:
Suppose you take a test with 3 questions and get 2 right (2/3). You passed with a solid 67%.
Now imagine the teacher doubles the test to 6 questions (multiplying the bottom by 2), but leaves your correct answers at 2 (not multiplying the top). Your score is now 2/6, which is 33%—you suddenly failed, even though you didn't get any more questions wrong.
To keep that exact same 67% score on a 6-question test, your correct answers have to double right along with the total questions (4/6).

Another way to see it: Money
Imagine a fraction is a vending machine price:
Top number: How many coins you have.
Bottom number: How many coins the snack costs.
If you have 2 coins and the snack costs 3 coins, you have 2/3 of the price.
Now, suppose the currency changes so every coin is cut in half—now the snack costs 6 half-coins (bottom ×2). If your coins weren't also split into 4 half-coins (top ×2), you would suddenly be way further away from buying the snack than you were a second ago.

The rule in one sentence: Multiplying the bottom makes the individual pieces smaller, so you must multiply the top by the same number to collect enough of those smaller pieces to make up for it.

it is 4/6 because you multiply the top and bottom by two Next one: 2/9 + 4/9?

Spot on—you nailed that!

For 2/9 + 4/9, the answer is 6/9 (which can also be simplified to 2/3).

How it works:
Check the bottom numbers (denominators): Since both fractions are already split into 9 equal pieces, the size of the pieces matches—so you don't need to change the bottom number at all. Just keep it as 9.
Add the top numbers (numerators): Simply add your pieces together: 2 + 4 = 6.

(Bonus tip: If your test asks you to simplify, both 6 and 9 divide cleanly by 3, which brings you right back to 2/3!)

Ready to throw another one at me, or want to try one with different bottom numbers?
I get that the top numbers add up, but why does the bottom number stay the same instead of becoming 18?

The bottom number isn't a number you're counting—it's the name of the object you're counting.

Think of the bottom number as a label, like "apples" or "ninths":
2 ninths + 4 ninths = 6 ninths (6/9)
Just like 2 apples + 4 apples = 6 apples (not 6 apple-apples!).

Why 18 would give the wrong answer:
If you added the bottom numbers to get 6/18, you would actually be shrinking your total:
2/9 is a bit less than a quarter of a pizza.
4/9 is almost half a pizza.
When you add them together, you should end up with more than half a pizza (6/9).
If you changed the bottom number to 18, each slice would suddenly become half as big! You'd end up with 6/18 (which simplifies to 1/3)—meaning you somehow lost pizza by adding two pieces together.

The golden rule for adding fractions:
Top number (Numerator): How many slices you have (this changes when you add).
Bottom number (Denominator): What size the slices are (this stays the exact same, because putting two slices on a plate doesn't magically chop them into smaller pieces).
